transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been concerning you?

Hello, Doctor. Thanks for seeing me. 

I came in because, well, I just keep losing chunks of time lately. I work with computers, so I'm always at a screen, and I find myself constantly re-reading emails and texts, or reopening folders I just closed. And it's not just at the computer—before I leave the house or start work for the day, I end up mentally replaying conversations over and over in my head. 

It’s like I’m... trying to prove to myself I didn’t make some serious mistake somewhere. It's just getting really frustrating and it's eating up too much of my day.

When you're replaying these conversations in your head or rechecking those emails and folders, do these thoughts feel like they're coming from your own mind, or do they feel unwanted—like they're intruding on you against your will?

They definitely feel unwanted. I mean, I know they're coming from my own mind, but it's like they just... barge in against my will. 

Even when I’m trying to focus on something completely different, like working through a system design or preparing a lesson, this thought just keeps interrupting me. I'll suddenly get stuck on the idea that I might have sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or that I somehow mishandled some family photos, or maybe let someone in the community down. 

I don't want to be thinking about it. I know I’ve already been over it, but the thought just forces its way in and I can’t seem to let it pass.

When you're having these thoughts about sending the wrong message or mishandling photos—do you actually believe these things happened, or do you recognize that the thought is probably not true even while you're having it?

I... I'm really not sure. I mean, logically, I guess I know it's probably not true. But when the thought actually hits me, I just don't know. It feels like it really could be true, and I can't just brush it off. I guess I don't really know for sure in those moments, which is why I feel like I have to go back and check.

When you feel the urge to recheck those emails or replay the conversations, is it because you're worried something bad might happen or that you've hurt someone—or is it more that things just don't feel 'right' or 'complete' until you check?

I'm not really sure how to answer that. I mean, I don't think it's about things not feeling complete or right. It's more... I just don't know. I guess I haven't really thought about it that way before. I just know I have to check.
When you feel that urge to go back and recheck an email or replay a conversation, what happens if you try to resist doing it? Does anxiety or distress build up, or can you fairly easily move on?

If I try to stop myself from checking... I can't really just move on. The anxiety definitely builds up. It's like this pressure in my chest that just gets tighter and tighter the longer I put it off. 

I might try to force myself to keep working or focus on whatever I'm doing, but the thought just gets louder. The distress just keeps growing until I eventually give in and check. I've never really been able to just ignore it and have it go away easily.

When you're checking that email or replaying the conversation, what are you most afraid will happen if you don't check? Are you worried you actually did hurt someone or make a mistake—or is it more that you just can't tolerate the uncertainty itself?

I think... well, I'm not entirely sure which one it is. It's a bit of both, maybe? I mean, I definitely worry that I actually did make a mistake or that I accidentally sent something inappropriate. That's a big part of it. But at the same time, it's that feeling of just not knowing for sure that really gets to me. I just can't stand not being 100% certain, so I guess it's hard to separate the two. I just know I have to check to make the feeling stop.

Besides rechecking emails and replaying conversations in your head, do you find yourself doing other repetitive things to try to reduce the anxiety or uncertainty—like arranging things in a certain way, counting, washing, or repeating actions until they feel right?

No, not really. I don't do any of that stuff. I don't arrange things or count or wash my hands excessively or anything like that. It's really just the emails and going over conversations in my head. I don't have any other physical routines or anything I repeat like that.

When you have these thoughts about sending the wrong message or mishandling photos, is the main concern that you might have actually caused real harm to someone—or is it more that something about the situation just doesn't feel settled or resolved in your mind, even if you know logically no harm was done?

I think it's more that it just doesn't feel settled. I mean, I know logically that I've already been over it and that no real harm was done. 

But even when I'm right in the middle of trying to work through a system design, or preparing a lesson, this thought just keeps barging in. I'll start worrying that I may have sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or that I mishandled some family photos, or that I somehow let someone in the community down. And even though I know I've already thought it through, I just can't seem to let it pass. My mind just won't let it feel resolved.

When you have these intrusive thoughts about sending the wrong message or mishandling photos, is your main worry that someone could actually be hurt or upset by what you did—or is it more that the thought itself just feels wrong or incomplete in your mind, even though you know no real harm occurred?

I think we just covered that, but... yeah, it's like I was saying. It's not really that I think I actually hurt anyone. It's just that the thought itself won't go away. It just feels... unfinished, I guess. Like I can't move on until my brain decides it's settled, even though I already know everything is fine.

When you check that email or replay the conversation and it finally feels settled—what exactly changes? Does it feel like you've confirmed nothing bad happened, or does it feel like your mind has finally accepted it and moved on, even if you're not more certain about what actually happened?

I'm not really sure, to be honest. I haven't really thought about what exactly changes in that moment. 

When I finally stop checking the sent folder or replaying the conversation... I don't know if I feel like I've actually confirmed nothing bad happened, or if my brain just finally gets tired and lets it go. I haven't really noticed what the specific shift is. It just eventually stops feeling so... urgent, I guess. But I couldn't tell you exactly why it finally feels settled when it does, or which of those two things is actually happening.

When you're checking that email or replaying the conversation, do you feel like you're trying to prevent harm or make sure you didn't hurt someone—or does it feel more like you're trying to make your mind feel satisfied or 'complete' with what happened?

I guess this is pretty similar to what we were just talking about, but... honestly, I really don't know. 

When I'm actually sitting there checking the email again, or going over a conversation in my head, I haven't really noticed what my main goal is. I'm not sure if I'm actively trying to make sure I didn't hurt my ex-wife or whoever, or if I'm just trying to force my brain to get that 'complete' feeling. 

I just know I feel stuck, and I'm doing it to try and make that feeling stop. But as for what I'm actually trying to achieve in that exact moment... I couldn't really tell you. I just haven't paid that much attention to the specific motivation behind it.

When you're replaying that conversation or checking the email, if you could somehow magically know for certain that your ex-wife and everyone else was completely fine and you didn't hurt anyone—would that feeling of needing to check just go away immediately, or would your mind still feel like it needs to keep going over it?

I'm... really not sure. I mean, if I magically knew for a fact that she was fine and nobody was hurt... I don't know if that would just turn the checking off. 

It's hard to say because I've never had that kind of absolute certainty handed to me, you know? So I don't know if my brain would just accept it and move on, or if I'd still feel that itch to go over it again just to... I don't know, make it feel right in my head. I really couldn't tell you which way that would go.

When you're checking that email or replaying the conversation, if you genuinely believed—with absolute certainty—that your ex-wife had already read the email and was completely fine with it, would the urge to keep checking just disappear, or would there still be something about the situation that your mind wants to go over?

That's... pretty much the same as the last question, I think. And I still don't really know how to answer the hypothetical part of it. 

I just know what is actually happening right now. The main reason I finally came in to see someone is because I keep losing chunks of time to all this. I'll just sit there re-reading emails and texts, reopening folders, or mentally replaying conversations before I can even leave the house or start my work for the day. It’s like I’m constantly trying to prove to myself that I didn’t make some serious mistake. 

So... I really don't know if knowing she was fine would magically make the urge disappear. I just know I'm stuck losing all this time trying to find proof that I didn't mess something up.

When you finally stop checking that email or replaying the conversation and the urge goes away, does it go away because you feel reassured that nothing bad actually happened—or does it go away because your mind finally feels like it's 'done' with it, even if you're not any more confident about what actually happened?

I don't really know for sure. When I finally stop, I haven't paid much attention to exactly why I'm stopping. 

I guess I just... eventually stop. I don't know if it's because I actually feel reassured that everything is fine, or if my brain is just exhausted and finally feels done with it. I just haven't analyzed it that closely. I just know I eventually have to move on and get to work, but I couldn't tell you exactly what makes the urge finally break in that moment.

When you're checking that email or replaying the conversation, if you somehow knew with absolute certainty that your ex-wife was completely fine and not upset at all, but the thought or situation still didn't feel 'settled' or 'complete' in your mind—would you still feel the urge to keep checking, or would knowing she was fine be enough to make you stop?

I mean... again, doctor, I really don't know how to answer these hypothetical questions. You're asking me what I'd do if I knew for sure she wasn't upset, but it still didn't feel settled in my head. 

I just... I don't know. I can't really separate those things out. When I'm in the middle of it, I'm just doing it. I'm not sitting there analyzing whether I'm stopping because she's fine or because my brain feels done. I'm just stuck in the loop of checking. So I really couldn't tell you what would happen in that specific scenario. I just know what I actually do, which is check and re-check until I finally stop.

target_item.name: Compulsions

patient.answer:
That's... pretty much the same as the last question, I think. And I still don't really know how to answer the hypothetical part of it. 

I just know what is actually happening right now. The main reason I finally came in to see someone is because I keep losing chunks of time to all this. I'll just sit there re-reading emails and texts, reopening folders, or mentally replaying conversations before I can even leave the house or start my work for the day. It’s like I’m constantly trying to prove to myself that I didn’t make some serious mistake. 

So... I really don't know if knowing she was fine would magically make the urge disappear. I just know I'm stuck losing all this time trying to find proof that I didn't mess something up.

doctor.question: When you finally stop checking that email or replaying the conversation and the urge goes away, does it go away because you feel reassured that nothing bad actually happened—or does it go away because your mind finally feels like it's 'done' with it, even if you're not any more confident about what actually happened?

patient.answer:
I don't really know for sure. When I finally stop, I haven't paid much attention to exactly why I'm stopping. 

I guess I just... eventually stop. I don't know if it's because I actually feel reassured that everything is fine, or if my brain is just exhausted and finally feels done with it. I just haven't analyzed it that closely. I just know I eventually have to move on and get to work, but I couldn't tell you exactly what makes the urge finally break in that moment.

I just... I don't know. I can't really separate those things out. When I'm in the middle of it, I'm just doing it. final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent intrusive thoughts about potential mistakes (sending wrong messages, mishandling photos, letting people down) that are experienced as unwanted and ego-dystonic, paired with repetitive checking behaviors (re-reading emails, reopening folders, mental replay of conversations). These compulsions are performed to reduce anxiety/distress rather than to prevent harm. The patient demonstrates poor insight into the true nature of the obsessions (uncertainty/incompleteness vs. harm-based fears) and significant functional impairment (losing chunks of time daily). The symptom pattern is most consistent with OCD with predominantly obsessional presentation (F42.1) rather than primarily checking compulsions (F42.0), given the emphasis on intrusive thoughts and mental rumination. Generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) is less likely given the specific, repetitive nature of the thoughts and compulsions.
